segments.text: "In southern Normandy, where my father and I lived, a German unit called the Lehr panzer had established its headquarters in this region.
My father had understood, for some time, that the Germans, during the occupation in France, favored beautiful residences.
It was during an exhibition, in the heart of our city, that he met a person who explained to him that his property was occupied by the Germans in the 1940s.
Obviously, it didn't take much for us to go to this gentleman's house.
Small isolated road in the woods, majestic gate, endless stone walls… the scene is set.
We pass in front of the caretaker's house and, opposite it, another building which seems dilapidated, with a false rear.
We are welcomed by the gentleman in question, and the visit begins…
What an atmosphere...
creaking parquet floors, old cabinets full of labeled fossils, dating from an even older era, and in this darkness, various small objects from the German army.
It’s truly a moment that remains engraved in our memories...
But the most surprising thing is to come, because in the other room, enthroned in the middle of this abandoned living room, there is a sort of small tank.
Disconcerting when you don't know what it is.
Once again, the Germans have developed a most inventive technology: it is a Goliath.
A wire-guided mini-tank which carried an explosive charge to be projected against buildings or enemy vehicles.
This Goliath was part of what is known as “Hitler’s special weapons”; it is a very rare and prized piece in the world of collecting.
Here in front of you is the gasoline engine version, and the entire interior is complete (without the explosive charge, obviously).
This Goliath is placed on its rack, provided for this purpose, which could contain four.
I will end with an unfortunate anecdote:
During the landing, in the Utah Beach sector, the Allies found small caves on the beaches, and inside these were stored Goliaths...
Not knowing what they were, thinking of ""toys"", some soldiers threw a grenade there...
and unfortunately died, because the explosion was increased tenfold by the charges."

segments.text: "Before you is an imposing souvenir from the Second World War, a weapon that reminds me that, when I was younger, with my brother, we tried – without any luck, of course – to play with it.
This weapon weighs nearly 20kg, and its technical name is as cold as its appearance: the PTRS 41.
A weapon from the East, which testifies to the fierce fight waged by the Soviet forces against the invaders.
As kids, we mostly asked ourselves: “But who can shoot with that?
It’s impossible, even for an adult…” Obviously, it was impossible to shoot standing up.
Prone shooting was obligatory.
This heavy rifle, through its robustness, embodied true brute force, conveying determination and the desire for protection against enemy tanks.
It's an anti-tank weapon!
Found in what was called “death row”, a dark place full of tragic memories, this PTRS-41 was used to pierce the armor of armored vehicles.
It represented a response to the metallic titans that threatened to devastate cities and reduce the tenacity of a people to ashes.
Imagine the soldiers on the Eastern Front, fighting in unforgiving conditions, where every shot could be the only defense between life and death, between freedom and captivity.
Anchored in the frozen ground of the battlefield, this rifle was a beacon of hope, cold but resolute.
Ironically, the German army itself sometimes adopted this instrument of destruction for its own purposes, recognizing the power contained in this Soviet device."

segments.text: "These 6 busts wear, with dignity, an authentic period jacket and helmet, representing the divisional units which landed on Omaha on June 6, 1944.

The first bust is adorned with the insignia of the First Infantry Division, also known as the Big Red One; the number 1 in red symbolizes this unit, which was part of the first waves of assault on Omaha.
Their motto: “No mission too difficult, no sacrifice too great: duty first.
Next to him, we find an ensemble of the 29th Infantry Division, represented by a yin-yang shaped badge in blue and gray colors.
These brave men, often citizen-soldiers with little experience, fought against tyranny by landing on the ….
Their motto is: “Let’s Go!”
The 3rd bust highlights the 5th and 2nd Rangers.
Their war cry: “Rangers lead the way” still resonates today among the tumultuous waves of Omaha.
This unit also suffered heavy losses with the 29th Division in the Vierville sector, while Colonel Rudder's men captured the cliffs of Pointe du Hoc, a few kilometers further on.
As you advance, the bust bearing the insignia of the 2nd Infantry Division is adorned with the head of an Indian chief, a symbol of strength and strategy.
Their motto: “No one’s 2nd”.
This unit landed on June 7 at Saint-Laurent-sur-Mer, on Omaha, and immediately began fighting; she will besiege Brest in August 44.
Next comes the entire Engineer Special Brigade.
This unit played a crucial role during the landing at Omaha: its mission was support and logistics.

Known for their tenacity and versatility, the men of these brigades worked under enemy fire: they came to lend a hand to the first assault waves, and their many heroic losses marked that bloody day in Omaha.
Finally, this last outfit bears the image of a typical Utah Beach airborne division: the 101st Division.

We have decided to present this jacket and this helmet with certain reservations, because, among our historical and local sources, we mention an event which would have occurred the day before June 6 in the town of Saint-Laurent...

A small group of a few men would have been parachuted in order to neutralize, in a specific area, Germans and to cut certain radio links; This operation would have been called “Operation Asquin” and would have been part of the Sussex agent infiltration program.

Local witnesses from the time relate these facts in an intimate way, and I keep a fairly open mind, since we have already found, in the sea and certain farms in the sector, material which historically had no place in the Omaha sector.
The future will certainly tell us more…

segments.text: "Among the powerful artifacts in our collection are the impressive ORIN… type sea mines, tangible witnesses of naval strategies during the Second World War.
These formidable machines, designed to destroy enemy ships, played a crucial role in controlling sea lanes, strongly impacting military operations and resupply efforts.
Found in a famous French port, these mines are a reminder of the constant and invisible threat that weighed on allied and enemy fleets.
Anchored beneath the water's surface, ORIN mines were equipped with sensitive triggers that responded to pressure or sound, detonating when a passing naval vessel passed.
They were arranged in dozens, thus protecting a strategic maritime passage.
Their installation along vital sea routes was intended to disrupt the transport of troops, weapons and supplies, directly influencing the course of operations and battles on the waters.
The impact of sea mines during the war was considerable: they wreaked havoc in the ranks of the naval forces, imposing caution and considerably slowing down maritime movements.
The measures to clear them and navigate safely mobilized significant human and technological resources, thus reflecting the strategic importance of these instruments of war.
Observing these relics on display, one can only imagine the stories of the sailors and crews who navigated these unseen perils, facing underwater dangers while fighting battles on the surface.
ORIN mines are not only weapons, but also symbols of psychological warfare waged on the seas, aimed at sowing terror and uncertainty.

Our presentation invites you to understand the complexity of naval warfare through these artifacts, which bear witness to the technical innovation and defensive and offensive tactics that marked the conflict.
By exhibiting them, we honor the memory of those who braved the risks inherent in naval combat, while reflecting on human ingenuity, once again put at the service of war."

segments.text: "Here is a mannequin which, by its outfit (you have certainly observed it slightly ajar), suggests a particular function.
She is in fact an undercover agent, member of the famous British Special Operations Executive (SOE), ready to “set Europe on fire from the inside”, as Churchill said.

The Special Operations Executive, from its establishment in 1940, recruited agents and trained them in subversive warfare: sabotage techniques, search for intelligence and disinformation, organization of resistance, infiltration by parachute.
The jump suit displayed in front of you is very interesting, because once removed, the agents wore civilian clothing underneath.
Once on the ground, they used a small shovel to bury the suit and integrate as normally as possible into rural or city life.
These agents were found from Norway to North Africa, via Eastern countries, where they worked to destabilize the Nazi regime.
Many women distinguished themselves within the SOE, and some suffered a tragic fate.
This was the case of “Claire Dumont”, a young French woman who was parachuted to the Loire, endowed with exceptional talent in linguistics and great determination.
In 1943, his mission was to infiltrate Nazi circles and transmit vital information to London, while orchestrating sabotage operations.
Thanks to her linguistic skills, she managed to pass herself off as a German sympathizer, thus gaining their trust.
One night, while she was carrying charges on a crucial railway line for the Germans, Claire was almost captured: her presence had been denounced by one of her collaborators...
However, she managed to escape at the last minute into the forest and found refuge with a farmer, himself a member of the resistance.
Despite the constant fear of detection, Claire continued to send coded messages to London.
She distinguished herself by organizing a new act of sabotage: the derailment of a German train.
The operation was a success, but attracted even more attention to herself.
The following days were marked by an intense hunt, but cunning, she used her ingenuity to escape the search...
Unfortunately, during a surprise raid, she was captured and interned in a prison notorious for SOE agents.
Despite weeks of brutal interrogations, she revealed no information about her networks.
His silence and resistance exasperated the Germans.
In retaliation, and to make an example, the Nazis decided to summarily execute him.
She was taken in the early morning to the prison courtyard.
Faced with her tormentors, Claire remained dignified and determined.
She addressed her last words to her fellow resistance fighters...
words of courage and perseverance in the fight for freedom.
She was shot shortly before the liberation of the region by Allied forces.

segments.text: "I now invite you to discover one of the most fascinating pieces in our collection: the Welbike, a small British motorcycle with an exceptional destiny.
Imagine yourself in the heart of World War II, in the 1940s: Allied forces are seeking to develop innovative ways to carry out military operations, often behind enemy lines.
It is in this context that the Welbike was born.
Designed by the Station IX unit of the British Secret Service, the Welbike is a motorcycle of disarming simplicity, but formidably effective.
It was developed specifically for paratroopers and special forces of the British army.
The idea is ingenious: to create a vehicle that is light, compact and easily transportable by air.
As soon as the whistle blows and the mission begins, the Welbike unleashes all its magic.
Parachuted into a cylindrical container, she reached the ground at the same time as the soldiers.
In just a few minutes, without complex tools, it is ready to hit the road.
Its designers have imagined a motorcycle which, in its compactness (only 32kg), still has a range of nearly 145 kilometers, thanks to its two-stroke gasoline engine.
If his frugal appearance often raises a smile, his contribution during the war is far from negligible.
The Welbike was used in various missions, notably during Operation Market Garden in the Netherlands in 1944.
Fast and discreet, it allowed soldiers to transport messages and cover long distances to establish strategic positions.
And now, before you, this remarkable piece is carefully preserved.
It embodies the ingenuity and determination of an era when each technological innovation could make the difference between the success and failure of a mission.
As an avid collector, I am honored to share this unique piece of history with you.
The Welbike remains a vibrant testimony to the spirit of resistance and inventiveness that marked the Second World War.
I hope that this discovery will have captivated you as much as it fascinates me.
Let’s continue our journey through history together…"

segments.text: "As you approach this scene, let your gaze rest on the mannequins meticulously arranged to recreate the poignant moment of the landing of American soldiers during the first wave of assault in June 1944.
Each face frozen in time embodies the courage of these young men who, driven by an unshakeable sense of duty, set foot on the beaches of Normandy.
Observe the details: the authentic uniforms, the weapons in hand, ready for the inevitable confrontation.
These soldiers, some barely out of adolescence, carried on their shoulders the weight of a world in search of freedom.
Omaha was the bloodiest landing beach: around 4,000 dead, missing and injured on June 6, 1944.
These large steel crosses, also called “Czech hedgehogs”, imposing and threatening, punctuate the sand, illustrating the formidable obstacles that each soldier had to overcome.
These pieces are austere symbols of enemy resistance, testifying to the brutality of the means of defense on this beach, transformed into a veritable theater of war.
This scene pays tribute to those who courageously faced the unknown, with fear in their bodies but hope in their hearts.
They wrote, in letters of fire and blood, the story of liberation, transforming the waves of anguish into sands of deliverance.
Take a moment to feel the emotion that emanates from this living painting, and think of the countless stories of bravery associated with it, forever engraved in the collective memory of humanity."

segments.text: "At the heart of our museum, a piece of medical history awaits you, evoking the challenges and innovations that marked war medicine.
Before you lies an American field hospital tent, a moving remnant of military operations that redefined medical practices amid the chaos of the front.
This tent, with all its carefully arranged utensils, tells the story of the first interventions on the ground during the Second World War.

The urgent need for rapid and effective care has led to significant advances in medical techniques; Field hospitals like this played a crucial role, bringing life-saving care close to the front lines, where every second counted.
Among the equipment on display, you will find one of the first X-ray machines used in the field.
This revolutionary device reflects the commitment of medical teams to providing rapid and accurate diagnoses, an innovation that has transformed the treatment of war injuries.
Thanks to these technical advances, doctors were able to immediately identify fractures and shrapnel invisible to the naked eye, greatly increasing the chances of survival of injured soldiers.
As you explore this room, you will also discover the essential tools and supplies that make up the arsenal of courageous doctors and nurses.

These objects, from the simple syringe to surgical instruments, are silent witnesses to the progress made in the field of medicine, from improved surgical techniques to the development of new methods of disinfection and treatment.
Medical practices in theaters of operations have evolved considerably thanks to these field structures.

The field hospital tent you are looking at is not only a place of memory, but also a vibrant tribute to the ingenuity and resilience of military medical professionals; their tireless work, faced with the horrors of war, paved the way for innovations that continue to influence our world today.

segments.text: "In front of this diorama of Vierville-sur-Mer, we will try to understand why this beach bears the name “Bloody Omaha”.
We know that Hitler expected the Allies to land in Europe from the west while the German army was busy on the eastern front.
In order to slow down or foil any attempt at a breakthrough to the west, he ordered the construction of the Atlantic Wall, from Norway to the Basque Country.
Normandy then saw its coasts fortified with bunkers, and a few months before the landing, these troops were reinforced in numbers.

The strategy envisaged on D-Day for the beaches of Omaha and Utah provided, even before the land landing operations, for aerial bombardments in order to neutralize the bunkers and other firing positions.
Unfortunately, at dawn, due to bad weather, the bombings took place behind enemy lines, leaving the defenses intact.
This is how the first assault waves landed under enemy fire.
The sea was then between two tides, providing an obvious field of fire for the Germans; some bunkers were oriented not towards the sea, but along the beach, which caused tragic losses.
Amphibious tanks had been designed to float and reach the beach.
Of the 32 tanks engaged, only 2 did not sink.
The only shelter the soldiers of the 29th, 5th Rangers and engineers could find were the beach defenses that the Germans had installed.
It was necessary to wait until the end of the morning for two ships to flank and offer their guns the opportunity to destroy the famous German defenses, finally allowing the troops to advance.
The toll in Omaha is tragic: around 4,000 dead, missing and injured.
This is the origin of the name given to “Bloody Omaha”."

segments.text: "In the complex twists and turns of World War II, the Enigma machine stood like an impregnable fortress of cryptography, daring anyone to break its carefully guarded secrets.
Designed by German engineers, the Enigma was an electromechanical encryption device used to encode military messages, rendering enemy communications incomprehensible and seemingly unhackable.

At the heart of this mind-blowing puzzle, each operator's keystroke on the Enigma's keyboard transformed the original message into a complex tangle of letters, changing daily according to carefully configured settings.
For the Allied war effort, deciphering these messages was crucial to thwarting Axis plans.
The challenge was taken up by a team of brilliant allied mathematicians and engineers, led by the famous Alan Turing.
It was in the center of Bletchley Park, England, that ingenious minds like Turing, Gordon Welchman and others devoted countless hours to understanding the mysteries of the Enigma.

With the valuable help of Polish mathematicians, who had already made significant advances on the Enigma before the outbreak of war, the British team built the Bombe machine, capable of quickly testing the many possible configurations of the Enigma.
Through their perseverance and ingenuity, the Allies were able to read the encrypted traffic of the German high command, turning the course of the war in their favor.
Their painstaking and often unrecognized work shortened the conflict and saved millions of lives, while laying the foundations of modern computing.
Now let me tell you about one of life's great coincidences...
During yet another flea market that my father was attending, he stopped in front of a stand which, at first glance, appeared to be selling a typewriter.
Obviously, he asked the seller what the price of this typewriter was.
The latter replied: 50 francs… My father grimaced a little and offered him 45.
Nothing to do, 50 francs, last price.
And so my father gave in and offered the sum of 50 francs for this “typewriter” which was none other than an “Enigma”.
Enigma has real historical weight and represents a very particular interest for collectors.
The story continues with this robbery which took place in this very museum, more than ten years ago.
The very day of the opening, four intruders entered the museum and kidnapped the cashier.
The sound of glass from the windows shattered, while one of the delinquents watched the cashier and the others stole a few things...
But above all, they took the Enigma machine.
Some time later, in a military surplus in Paris, some young people showed up and offered to sell an Enigma machine.
The only proof: a photo.
The manager of the establishment could not believe his eyes.
He arranged to meet these young people with the machine to offer them a very nice sum.
Once they left, the situation seemed too strange to be true; he therefore contacted the police to explain to them what he had just witnessed.
The authorities obviously informed him that a museum had recently been robbed and that an Enigma machine had been stolen.
An ambush was then organized, and the delinquents stupidly fell into the trap.
The Enigma machine was found intact.

segments.text: "This showcase is dedicated to some objects from the British army, found in various places in the English sectors of D-Day.
This reminds me of my uncle who, even as a child, told us his anecdotes, shared with my father in the small bar near “Pégasus Bridge” — witnesses of a time when bravery crossed borders and the skies.
The last free bastion of a Europe occupied in the 1940s, England will remain a fault line in the Nazi regime through which the path to liberation will begin.
On the right, here is a box of homing pigeons.
In the air, these winged messengers carried hope and crucial information, crossing enemy lines to ensure the coordination of allied operations.
They were true soldiers of silence, saving lives with the simple flapping of their wings.
The English paratrooper helmet, marked with a medical unit, has become very rare to find.
This helmet covered the heads of those who, flying through the skies, plunged into hostile territories.
At the dawn of D-Day, they jumped into the unknown above places that have become mythical, like Pegasus Bridge, carrying a destiny greater than themselves.
These silk maps, so light and yet so vital for navigating enemy territory, were designed to survive bad weather, or even in the event of a plane crash.
They guided our Allies through uncertain landscapes in their mission.
The weapon you see here is a PIAT, a British anti-tank weapon, proof of the power hidden in the determined hands of English soldiers.
Unreliable, imprecise, it nevertheless embodied the resistance necessary to repel enemy armored forces.

The typical English battle dress jacket, displaying the insignia of the paratroopers, evokes those nights when the black sky was populated with floating silhouettes: these reckless fighters descending to extend their hand to freedom.
The Fairbairn commando dagger, a Lee-Enfield rifle, a scuba diving unit...
all these objects have been found over the years, giving rise to research, exchanges and investments.
Personally, I am amazed at how the English were true pioneers in many areas.
Their innovations, both technologically and historically, continue to make history today."

segments.text: "In the family home, a few years after the death of our father, an incredible discovery awaited me.
Buried under the weight of years and the silence of kept secrets, it was by an incredible chance, on an ordinary day, that my gaze lingered on a trapdoor in the floor of a hangar.
A hatch which, at first glance, seemed quite ordinary.
By opening the base, I discovered a slight recess of about 40 cm, a pipe fitted with a tap and a bottom covered with gravel.
I just didn't understand the presence of this pipe.
Don't ask me why, but in a completely innocuous gesture, I started stirring the gravel that was at the bottom...
What was my surprise when I discovered a lock.
I stood stunned, trying to understand.
It must have opened a drawer, but nothing moved.
In the excitement of this discovery, I remembered that, among all the keys to the property, I had come across a particularly strange key.
She was very tall, with a huge ring.
Without a second thought, I run to look for it...
Once in the lock, I try maneuvers to articulate it, I look for a direction...
then, suddenly, the drawer slides heavily towards me.
It was not a drawer, but an entrance!
A black hole presented itself to me with a ladder.
My heart was palpitating; I was amazed because I had known the house since childhood: I had searched and played everywhere.
If there was anyone who knew the house by heart, it was me… Well, I thought so.
I still can't believe it.
I go down… we don’t see anything.
Feet first, then hands.
Once on this narrow ladder, an old electrical box is to my left: I press…
And there...
a room not very big, but filled with weapons from the Second World War: MGs, Mausers, endlessly.
Around 200 weapons were stored.
And in the middle of it all, the weapon in front of you: an FG 42.
A German paratrooper machine gun, produced in only 2500 copies.
It is an item highly coveted by collectors.
For example, one day, after visiting the museum, someone almost offered us €100,000 to leave with this machine gun.
I later learned, by cross-checking various testimonies among my father's acquaintances, that this piece aroused a lot of jealousy around him.
It is for this reason that this cache was built, during his spare time, making it impossible for the FG to steal.
I had also learned that this little treasure came from the “death row cliff pocket”.
My father and uncle were among the first to excavate and collect relics from the Second World War.

As I descended into this little-known lair, I felt more than ever the weight of the family heritage and the call to discover what had motivated their determination to create such a space, to hide these precious things.

segments.text: "This window is dedicated to an era of courage: that of the French Resistance during the Second World War.
Each of the objects present here tells the story of those who, in the shadows, fought for freedom and dignity.
On the right, you can see various trapping elements: these ingeniously designed explosive devices, used to disrupt the advance of the occupying forces...
The railways, for example, suffered a lot of damage as a result of these actions.
Knives, silent but formidable tools in close combat, constituted either a last defense or a means of furtive strike.
They belonged to men and women ready to sacrifice everything.
The leaflets that you can see here served to raise awareness and rally free spirits.
Distributed at the risk of their lives, these papers were real cries of revolt against oppression, calls to stand up for a better homeland.

The green beret of the KIEFFER commandos symbolizes the unity and courage of the 177 French soldiers who responded to the call of June 18, fighting side by side with their allies to liberate a country reduced to silence.
The detonators, tire slashes and this modified Mauser weapon testify to the inventiveness of the resistance fighters.

And then, there are the fake stamps, essential instruments for creating false identities: real keys to survival, allowing many resistance fighters to escape the clutches of the enemy and continue their fight in the shadows.
Faced with limited resources, they transformed their environment, using each piece, each tool, to fuel their endless struggle.
We were fortunate to know several resistance fighters during their lifetime.
Through their stories, they passed on to us the objects they kept in a corner of their house.
We perpetuate their memory through this window, because it is a real childhood memory of having met these people, who did not wear a uniform—apparently simple citizens...
But what audacity!
What audacity to have resisted!
Their bravery and determination continue to inspire, reminding us that even in the darkest hours, the light of resistance never goes out."

segments.text: "Here begins...
stories of women and men, anecdotes of historical facts, and sometimes dramas.
This place houses a collection full of stories, which testifies to man's relationship with his past.
This place is also very important, because it was the first field hospital established on the beaches of Omaha after the landing of the first assault waves, many of which met a tragic fate.
But let me introduce ourselves: we are two brothers, Fabien and Antoine.
We grew up with a dad… quite special.
A true history buff, who devoted most of his life to searching for vestiges of this period.
We spent our youth, my younger brother and I, through forests, rivers and old barns, searching for all the traces left by the belligerents of the Second World War.
But at what cost...
Our father was obsessed, even obsessed!
by this passion...
It had become a permanent madness which, over the years, destroyed our family and himself.
He died in 2012, consumed by certain demons resulting from the vices of possession, consumed by remorse for having turned his back on the values ​​of family and friendship.
With the sudden departure of our father and our different paths, the future and the soul of this place found themselves compromised.
It was an elusive instinct that convinced my brother and me to continue our adventure through the search for historical objects, and to present them to you with their history.
Because, believe me, you will not be disappointed.
Welcome to our story.
Welcome to history."

segments.text: "Here we are in front of a captivating scene rich in history: an impressive Focke-Wulf engine, this formidable German fighter from the Second World War, accompanied by two models of Luftwaffe pilots.
This engine, the central piece of the scene, embodies a unique story that I am happy to share with you today.
It was while browsing the pages of a newspaper that my gaze lingered on a fascinating article.
The story took place in a small village where, during development work in front of the station, an improbable discovery took place: several German aviation engines, Focke-Wulf.
Driven by audacity and an unwavering passion for history, I contacted the mayor of the town to express my desire to preserve one of these historic pieces in our museum.
Invited to visit the engine storage location, the next stage of my quest finally took place on a farm.
But, among the four engines initially exhibited, only one was still present.
The others had been stolen, taking with them so many fragments of the past.
However, destiny led me to this one: the most beautiful, preserved in obscurity, safe from covetousness.
This Focke-Wulf engine is a true engineering masterpiece.
Designed for extreme performance, it embodied the cutting-edge technology of its time, allowing the aircraft to achieve dizzying speeds and exceptional maneuverability, crucial in aerial duels.
Its advanced design and power bear witness to the ambitions and technical skills mobilized on the battlefields of the air.
Surrounded by two Luftwaffe pilots, motionless and silent, this engine seems to resonate with the roar of the air it has crossed.
It encapsulates the strength and complexity of the era's aerial technology, testifying to humanity's relentless efforts to reach the skies, even in times of war.
In front of this vestige, we affirm our commitment to preserving history in all its authenticity.

segments.text: "Hidden among the relics of history, in an area tragically nicknamed “death row” in Normandy, was a precious piece of World War II: an anti-tank gun called the PAK 40, still adorned with its authentic period three-tone camouflage.

Discovered by my father and I in the late 1980s, thanks to the memory and kindness of a local farmer, this PAK 40 is now a centerpiece of our collection, displayed to provide a striking insight into German artillery during the Battle of Normandy.
The PAK 40 was one of the most feared anti-tank guns in the German arsenal.
Designed to pierce the thick armor of Allied tanks, it played a key role in defending German forces against mechanized assaults.

Its 75mm caliber and its ability to rapidly fire several types of ammunition allowed it to cause considerable havoc among enemy armored units, slowing their progress and inflicting substantial losses.
Its maximum firing range was approximately 7km.
This cannon transports us directly to 1944, to the heart of the Normandy countryside, where the concealed or ambush positions made it a deadly and effective weapon.

The camouflage, specially designed to confuse the artillery with the landscape, reminds us how cunning and ingenuity were essential in the art of war, making each ambush potentially fatal for the Allied forces.
Unfortunately, I cannot reveal how it was found, nor the precise location of its discovery, because it belongs to another era...
The echoes of the battles, which once resonated in this “death row”, jealously guard their secrets."

segments.text: "Before you stands the imposing Flakvierling 38, a powerful witness to the military ingenuity of the Second World War.
Designed by German forces, this four-barrel 20mm anti-aircraft gun tore through the sky with a lightning rate of fire, projecting a wall of fire against Allied aircraft.
This metal monster, sometimes nicknamed ""the shredder of the sky"", was found in Germany, symbol of a time when the shadow of conflicts stretched across the entire world.
Its imposing presence recalls the moments when, in a deafening noise, it split the skies to defend German territory from incessant aerial assaults.
Placed on a trailer for optimal mobility or on vehicles such as half-tracks, these guns could be moved wherever the need arose, their versatility transforming battlefields.
The ground itself vibrated with the intensity of each salvo, redefining the rules of aerial engagement.
But the Flakvierling 38 didn't just threaten the metal birds that pierced the clouds.
Its ability to strike land targets also made it a formidable adversary for advanced forces, which had to deal with merciless gusts.
Today we are faced with the duality of human technology: capable of the best and the worst.
This canon, deliberately forgotten by time, reminds us of the fragility of peace and the price paid by so many lives under its thunder of fire.

segments.text: "I am delighted to share with you, in this special section of our audio guide, not only historical facts, but also some of my personal passion for collecting military uniforms.
Today I'm going to talk to you about German camouflage used during World War II, a subject that is particularly close to our hearts.
As a collector, each piece I discover tells a unique story.
German camouflage outfits are no exception.
Crafted with meticulous attention to detail, they reflect a fascinating blend of functionality, innovation and adaptation to various theaters of war.
With their haphazard patterns and earthy colors, they provided effective camouflage in European environments.
We find aspects corresponding to all seasons: if you look closely, you will see spring and autumn variations for cold regions, white for winter, and summer colors for our more temperate regions.
There is also the ""polka dot"" motif, introduced later in the conflict.
Its complexity recalls the constant determination to improve the stealth of soldiers.
This unique pattern illustrates how innovation was essential in these troubled times.
In our collection, a jacket bearing this motif was mainly worn by SS members of the Hitler Youth, who held Caen for more than a month, while initial estimates spoke of two days.
The Germans placed enormous importance on camouflage.
History shows us that the Allies also tried to use similar camouflage...
but the resemblance unfortunately created confusion.
The Allies therefore very quickly abandoned the idea.
What is fascinating is to imagine how these camouflages were perceived at the time.
For the soldiers who wore them, it was more than just a piece of clothing: it was a vital part of their survival equipment.
In those days, technological means did not make it possible, as a satellite or a drone would do today, to detect the concealment of people or equipment.
Only the sense of sight was required.

segments.text: "1989… I am 9 years old.
My brother Fabien and I are huddled in this freezing tent, waiting for daylight to dawn on this Norman land.
Today, we are perhaps going to make a most relevant discovery.
Indeed, my father does a lot of research in Normandy, looking for vestiges and traces of history.

We are precisely in a place where, according to the testimony of a farmer, an American soldier stole a strange vehicle from the Germans and abandoned it hastily in a shell hole, his attackers being in pursuit.
The time has finally arrived: it is light enough to start digging.
There are five of us: my brother, me, my father, one of his friends and the person who operates the machine.
Min…nothing!
Min, still nothing!
But the sound of the detector is getting louder and louder.
After three minutes, the first very characteristic sound of metal meeting another metal.
We are obsessed by this noise and by the shape which becomes clearer as the shovel hits.
Our heads tilt over this hole trying to understand the silhouette of what is buried in the earth.
The sound of metal knocking and scratching with each maneuver makes us terribly excited: we almost forget the cold and humidity.
We are drunk on action, as if we could go faster than a shovel.
We were just kids...
Suddenly, after clearing a huge block of earth on the side, we see a piece of caterpillar—but not as I imagined at that age.
I knew very well what a tank caterpillar looked like… and this one was very small.
I didn't understand.
My father understood very well what it was about, and decided to dig a square around it, measuring about three meters by two meters.
Once these trenches were made, we began to remove all the blocks of earth by hand...
and little by little, a shape almost out of a science fiction film appeared to us.
My brother and I understood absolutely nothing about what was taking shape in front of us: caterpillars, motorcycle handlebars, a box with seats… We were lost.
My father knew very well what we had just found: a German motorcycle caterpillar, or Kettenkrad, a German reconnaissance vehicle used during the Second World War.
Here is the story of this strange vehicle before your eyes.
And to conclude...
the farmer's story was indeed true, because, as we can still see, there is a piece of fabric camouflaged in the caterpillars.
It is none other than a piece of American parachute, which undoubtedly allowed this soldier to hide the caterpillar motorcycle under his own parachute canopy.

segments.text: "Before you is the outfit of a German chaplain from World War II.
These men of faith occupied a unique place within the German army, responsible for providing spiritual support to soldiers immersed in the harsh reality of war.
Chaplains could be Catholic or Protestant, each offering the comfort of their religious tradition to the soldiers of their faith.
The chaplains lived a daily paradox.
In their role of support and comfort, they wore an outfit marked with symbols evoking a dark and complex period in our history today.

These symbols, although affixed to their uniform, did not necessarily define the personal convictions of these men, whose primary mission was to provide spiritual and moral refuge in the surrounding chaos.
Often working in extremely difficult conditions, German chaplains tried to improve the daily lives of soldiers, offering listening and compassion in the face of moral and emotional trials.
Their daily challenge?
Maintaining the light of humanity and faith in an environment often devoid of moral guidelines.
As representatives of the two main Christian denominations, they also had the task of promoting a certain moral unity within the troops, in a context where divisions and suffering were omnipresent.

In presenting this outfit, it is crucial to recognize all dimensions of history: the personal commitment of the chaplains and the contexts that shaped them, while being aware of the symbols and ideologies they wore.
It reminds us of the importance of questioning and understanding our past."

segments.text: "In a country house nestled in the south of Normandy, an unexpected treasure was discovered during a morning full of mystery and emotion.
This find, much more than a simple toy, is a doll.
A “Rupert” doll, guardian of a little-known story from the Second World War.
In appearance, Rupert looks like any doll of the time, with his worn clothes and almost non-existent facial features.
However, what makes this doll truly poignant is its singular role in the history of the resistance and allied operations.
During Operation TITANIC, a daring mission to deceive Nazi forces before the Normandy landings, hundreds of similar dolls, called “Ruperts,” were dropped from the sky.
They were equipped with sound devices and small explosives, mimicking the presence of paratroopers and sowing confusion and disinformation behind enemy lines.

As you stop in front of this relic, I can't help but think that certain elite soldiers accompanied the parachuting of these dolls, firing machine guns and broadcasting various sound effects to make the diversion as close to reality as possible.

Regardless, this discovery in this attic with my father invites us to think that this doll is truly a tangible illustration of how the most innocent objects can play a crucial role in grand war strategies.
These stories are those of invisible soldiers, ingenious stratagems and tense nights.
This doll, so frail and innocent, reminds us that, even in the darkest times, cunning always finds a way to shine.

segments.text: "The story takes place on a shooting range of a French institution…
Come see!
- Where are you ?
Come this way!
- But what are you doing???
Listening !!!
This gives you an idea of ​​the rate of fire of this German machine gun, the MG42.
You imagine, on June 6, American and allied soldiers landing under enemy fire, and this fire also bore the name of MG42...

History will unfortunately remember the one who has been called “the Beast of Omaha”: Heinrich Severloh, who, on the day of June 6, 44, held his position behind his MG42 from one of the strategic bunkers of Omaha.
He claims, in his stories, to have fired around 12,500 cartridges.
It's scary.
He will recount, in his memoirs, that he did not shoot for pleasure, but to stay alive.
